processing: Little is recorded about this estate's methods; Dibrugarh gardens generally make fully oxidised orthodox and CTC black tea.
harvest_season: No garden-specific calendar is documented; as with other Assam gardens, the May to June second flush is generally the most valued.
appearance_dry: Typical of Assam black tea: dark leaf, in whole or broken grades.
appearance_liquor: Reddish amber, as is usual for Assam.
appearance_wet: Coppery brown leaf, typical of the class.
taste_profile: No dependable tasting record exists for this garden; Dibrugarh black teas are generally malty and full-bodied.

brewing.notes: Brew like any Assam black tea and adjust by taste. Milk is a sensible option.

vintage_note: Rarely seen abroad under its own name, and no year or flush pattern is documented for it. As usual for Assam, drink it within a year or two of picking; guests can also taste estate tea at the heritage bungalow.
description:
Mancotta is a Dibrugarh tea estate in Upper Assam, and it is far better known for where you can stay than for what is in the cup. Its stilted colonial bungalow, the Mancotta Chang, is now a heritage stay.

Little is recorded about the tea itself. Gardens around Dibrugarh generally make fully oxidised black tea, both orthodox and CTC, so assume that until a pack tells you otherwise.

A typical Dibrugarh cup is malty and full-bodied. Three grams, hot water and three to four minutes make a reasonable start.

This is a tea best met on site: visitors drink estate tea on the veranda and can cycle through the plantation. Should you find a pack elsewhere, look for a grade and a date.
history:
The bungalow was once home to British planters and now belongs to the Jalan family, whose tea business goes back to the middle of the 19th century. Its age is given differently in different accounts: built in the late 1800s, or over 150 years old as of 2014.

The estate's founding date and first planters are not reliably documented.
